chapter: The 1920s road: dance style and management
title: Making entertainment clean for the Negro
summary: He says he made it clean for Negro entertainers and that Redd Foxx or Richard Pryor would not have been booked then, while Buck and Bubbles had everything.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: But that's the way life goes. Who's going to know how to do life -- nobody. So you see, George, when you talk about show business I'm thinking -- see, what hurts me more or less about this business is I was in it so long and made it clean for the negro with entertainment that the negro was received. People like Redd Foxx wouldn't have been received in the theaters in those days because he has a dirty act. They wouldn't book him. And neither would they book what's-his-name? Richard Pryor? Him, neither. And most of them didn't have nothing -- what's his name -- Jones? You know the fella I'm talking about, he did the White Hope. (James Earl Jones). What's his name -- you know who I mean. Well, him, he had nothing to offer. You have to have something to offer, man. You couldn't just get on 'cause you think you ought to be on the stage. No, no, you had to have something else. And Buck and Bubbles had everything. Everything. We had humor. We had personality. We had reasoning power.
